newsitem.title: USA: Sweet terms woo investors to Mexico global bond.
newsitem.headline: Sweet terms woo investors to Mexico global bond.

text.p: Mexico will price its new global bond in a way that ensures room for gains to cultivate the good will of investors for future funding needs, market sources said.
"Mexico may want to leave something on the table to ensure the new securities will trade well after-market," said Tulio Vera, a managing director of Bear Stearns.
Syndicate sources said the $1 billion, 10-year fixed rate global bond would be priced 337.5 basis points (bp) over U.S. Treasuries.
When the offering was announced on Friday, market sources estimated the spread at 310-315 bp or lower.
Mexican officials in the New York roadshow told investors the size of this deal would not be increased, according to market sources who attended the presentation.
Pricing and allocation will be made on Thursday.
Despite ample liquidity in the market, investors' risk appetite turned out to be more conservative than expected, said a buy-side source.
"Investors were not interested at 300 (bp) and the underwriters got the message," he said.

Recent volatility in the U.S. interest rates has raised the level of uncertainity for the high-yield papers, prompting investors to demand a greater cushion on the spread, said Omar Borla, chief Latin America economist at Robert Flemings, Inc.
"Instability in the (U.S.) Treasuries magnifies the country risk there," he said.
The amount of the supply in the market, taking into account Argentina's $2 billion global offer announced Tuesday, also put pressure on the spread, he added.

Mexican officials at the roadshow emphasized the economic recovery was on track, forecasting in 1997 a four percent growth in gross domestic product, 15 percent inflation and a fiscal deficit of 0.5 percent of the GDP, market sources said.
They estimated the 1997 current account deficit at $6 billion to $7 billion, which would be more than covered by some $8 billion of foreign direct investment, according to the sources.
The Mexican government's assumption of average oil price oil price is $14.50 a barrel, they said.
"They present a credible economic picture," said an analyst who attended the presentation.
Nancy Northrop, vice president of emerging markets at Alliance Capital Management Corp, expected the deal to be well received on those terms.
"The trend for inflation is down and the government is committed to meeting the fiscal target," she said.
